opus-5.5.text:
I think the overlap is much bigger than people assume, and honestly it's been growing every year.

If you look at the people, a lot of the folks now building embodied intelligence, whether it's humanoids, mobile manipulation, or general robot foundation models, came out of autonomous driving. That's not an accident. Autonomous driving was really the first place where the industry had to take a physical AI system out of the lab and make it work at scale, in the real world, with real safety consequences. So that community built up a lot of muscle: how you set up a data flywheel, how you collect and label huge amounts of sensor data, how you build simulation and closed-loop evaluation, how you handle the long tail. Those lessons transfer almost directly.

On the technical side, the convergence is even clearer. A few years ago driving was this modular pipeline: perception, prediction, planning, control, each with its own team. Then the field moved toward end-to-end models, and now people talk about vision-language-action models and world models for driving. That's essentially the same vocabulary the embodied-intelligence people use. In a sense, a car is just a robot with a very constrained action space. You're outputting a trajectory, steering and acceleration. A humanoid or a robot arm has a much higher-dimensional action space and much richer contact with the world, but the underlying question is the same: how do you go from perception to action through a model that actually understands the physical world?

That said, I don't think it's a simple "copy and paste" from driving to robotics. There are some real differences.

The first one is data. Driving has a natural data source: there are millions of cars on the road, and you can collect fleet data almost for free as a byproduct of people driving. Robotics doesn't have that yet. There's no installed base of robots doing useful work in homes or factories at scale, so data collection is expensive. You're doing teleoperation, you're doing simulation, you're trying to learn from human videos. That changes the whole strategy.

The second is the task definition. Driving, at the end of the day, is one task with a pretty clear objective: get from A to B safely and comfortably. Embodied intelligence is open-ended. You want a robot that can fold laundry, load a dishwasher, assemble something on a line. Generalization matters in a completely different way.

The third is evaluation. In driving, we've spent years figuring out metrics, scenario libraries, and safety cases. In robotics, evaluation is still kind of messy. Everyone shows a demo video, but it's hard to compare systems rigorously. I actually think this is one area where people from driving can contribute a lot, because they know how painful it is to ship something that looked great in a demo but failed in the long tail.

So my view is that the two communities are converging into one bigger field, maybe you'd call it physical AI. Driving is the most mature application, and it's a kind of training ground for talent and methodology. Embodied intelligence is where the problem gets much more general and much harder. And I think the ideas will flow in both directions. Things like world models and large-scale pretraining that are being pushed hard in robotics will likely feed back into driving as well.

r001.rationale: The response says that many people now building embodied intelligence “came out of autonomous driving.”

fable-5.1.text:
There's a huge overlap, honestly more than people outside realize. If you look at who's building embodied-intelligence companies right now, a very large share of them came out of autonomous driving. And that's not an accident. Autonomous driving was, in a sense, the first large-scale embodied AI problem that actually got funded and deployed. A car is a robot. It perceives the physical world, it makes decisions under uncertainty, and it acts in real time where mistakes have consequences.

So the technical toolkit transfers almost directly. Perception, sensor fusion, the whole data engine idea, closed-loop simulation, long-tail mining, how you structure a data flywheel between the fleet and the training pipeline. The people who spent eight or ten years learning those lessons the hard way in driving are now carrying them into robotics.

But there are real differences, and I think the driving people sometimes underestimate them. A car lives in a highly structured world. There are lanes, traffic rules, a limited action space, basically steering and acceleration. A robot in a home or a factory has an open-ended action space, contact-rich manipulation, deformable objects, and an environment nobody standardized. The physics is much harder, and the data is much scarcer. In driving you can get millions of hours from the fleet almost for free. In manipulation, every hour of good data is expensive, and that changes how you think about everything.

The other direction is interesting too. The end-to-end wave in driving, moving from modular pipelines to large models that go from sensors to actions, actually got a lot of its confidence from what the embodied and foundation-model communities were showing. So the ideas are flowing both ways now.

My view is that over the next few years these two communities will increasingly look like one community, with driving being one application of a more general physical intelligence stack. The talent is already mixing, the conferences are mixing, and the model architectures are converging. The main thing that still separates them is the data problem, and whoever solves that for general robots will probably define the field.

r001.rationale: The response says a very large share of embodied-intelligence company builders came out of autonomous driving and are bringing those lessons into robotics.

astra-6.text:
I think the overlap is substantial. Autonomous driving is already a form of embodied intelligence: a system has to perceive the world, predict what might happen, make decisions, and act—and those actions change what it observes next.

So the two communities share many problems, especially around learning from data, simulation, and evaluating safety. People working on autonomous driving have experience building that entire loop, which is valuable for robotics.

But the transfer isn’t automatic. A car operates within a relatively defined set of actions, mainly steering, accelerating, and braking. A robot manipulating objects has to deal with contact, force, and many more degrees of freedom. Even defining whether a task succeeded can be more complicated.

To me, the strongest connection is the way you approach the problem: how do you turn a model that performs well on a dataset into a system that reliably acts in the physical world? That’s where these communities have a lot to learn from each other.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous-driving experience is valuable for robotics, but it does not state that many people have moved from autonomous driving into embodied intelligence.

sol-6.1.text:
I see a substantial overlap, because both are trying to connect perception, decision-making, and action in the physical world. An autonomous vehicle is, in that sense, a form of embodied intelligence. It has to understand its surroundings, predict what other agents might do, and act under uncertainty.

But the operating environments and action spaces differ. Driving has a relatively structured set of rules, even though the situations can be extremely complex. A robot working in a home may face a much wider range of objects and tasks, with contact and manipulation becoming central challenges.

So there’s a lot the communities can learn from each other: how to collect useful interaction data, how to combine learning with control, and how to evaluate systems beyond a compelling demonstration. The strongest overlap, to me, is the need to close the loop—what matters is whether the system can act reliably and recover when the world behaves differently than it expected.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared goals and lessons between the communities but does not state that many people from autonomous driving have moved into embodied intelligence.
